title: MLB's Smallest Market Just Won It All. How?
description:
Milwaukee is the smallest TV market in Major League Baseball, and on Oct 28, 2026 the Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 to win the first World Series in franchise history. We go through the five games (including a record eight two-out runs in one inning), the payrolls (Brewers about $146M, Rays about $95M, Dodgers about $412M by SB Nation's figures), how both teams build rosters through trades and homegrown players, the Rays' year after Hurricane Milton, and why both sides of baseball's Dec 1 labor fight now point to this series. Real players appear only as generic labelled stick figures; quotes are as reported.

We don't pick sides. We just count the facts.

#worldseries #brewers #rays #mlb #baseball #explained #stickfigure

scenes.say: On Wednesday night, thirty-one thousand people filled a baseball stadium in Milwaukee.
The game was in Florida.
They paid to sit in their own ballpark and watch a screen, more than a thousand miles from the actual game.
Then, at eleven thirteen p.m., a ground ball to second base. The Milwaukee Brewers won the World Series. The first title in the team's history.
Milwaukee is the smallest TV market in Major League Baseball. Thirtieth out of thirty.
So here's the puzzle. In a sport with no salary cap, where the rich can outspend everyone, how does the smallest city win the whole thing?
We'll go through the five games, the money, the trades, the other team's strange year, and the fight about to start in December.
First, what happened. The Brewers played the Tampa Bay Rays. Two teams that finished with the best records in their leagues.
Milwaukee won a hundred and three games this season. A franchise record, and the best in baseball.
Game one, in Milwaukee: Brewers three, Rays two. Decided on the last pitch.
Game two: the Rays led four to nothing. Milwaukee chipped away and won by one run again.
Game three, in Florida, was the strange one. In the fifth inning, with two outs, Milwaukee scored eight runs.
Seven hits in a row, all with two outs. According to the AP, no World Series team had ever scored eight two-out runs in one inning.
Final score: ten to one. A Brewers rookie pitcher said that normally it's thirty-five thousand against nine, but that night they had twenty thousand people behind them.
Game four went twelve innings. Milwaukee was three outs from the title. The Rays came back and won it at the very end.
Dave watched that one from his couch. He says he aged three years. His wife says it was more like five.
Game five, back in Florida: Brewers four, Rays one.
Their starting pitcher threw fifty-one fastballs at a hundred miles an hour or faster, according to the AP, before a calf cramp ended his night.
Three relievers finished the job. Final out: a ground ball to second. That's the one the people in Milwaukee watched on the big screen.
Over five games, the Brewers outhit Tampa Bay fifty-one to thirty and outscored them twenty-five to twelve.
The series MVP was the catcher, William Contreras. Eight hits in twenty-one at-bats.
scenes.chapter: Part 2: The stars nobody paid for

scenes.say: A rookie shortstop, Cooper Pratt, hit four twenty-one in the series and set a rookie record: hits in six straight World Series at-bats.
He didn't play his first big-league game until June sixteenth. Four months later, he's in the record book.
And the captain, Christian Yelich, who arrived in twenty eighteen, said it felt like a movie.
Their manager, Pat Murphy, said, we came in with a spirit about us, and we weren't going to be denied.
Notice something about this list? Almost nobody on it is a superstar who signed for a fortune.
Now the money. Major League Baseball has no salary cap. Each team spends what its owner wants to spend.
According to SB Nation's figures, Milwaukee's payroll is about a hundred forty-six million dollars. Nineteenth in the league.
Tampa Bay's is about ninety-five million. Depending on which list you use, somewhere between twenty-fifth and twenty-eighth.
For comparison, the same article estimates the Los Angeles Dodgers' payroll at about four hundred twelve million.
Put the two finalists together, and CBS Sports says their payroll rankings are the lowest ever for a World Series.
And the smallest combined market for a World Series since nineteen eighty-five.
Both teams also receive more money from baseball's revenue sharing than they pay in. CBS says that can cover most or all of a low-payroll team's cash payroll.
Which is a polite way of saying part of the bill was paid by richer teams. Those teams will be bringing that up.
Quick one. If ten calm minutes of stick figures beat an hour of shouting sports radio for you, subscribe. That's the whole service.
So how do you build a champion on a medium budget? Mostly, you trade.
scenes.chapter: Part 4: How you build it cheap

scenes.say: CBS Sports counted twenty-two players on Milwaukee's forty-man roster who came by trade. Tampa Bay had twenty-four, the most in baseball.
Their MVP catcher came in a trade. So did the captain, back in twenty eighteen.
The other half is growing your own. Players Milwaukee drafted and developed produced just over half of the team's value this season, by one common stat.
CBS says both teams share a style. Hitters who make contact instead of swinging for the moon. Pitchers who throw hard. Big scouting departments.
And they're cousins. Milwaukee's head of baseball operations spent nine years in Tampa Bay's front office before moving north.
So the World Series was, in a way, the student against the school.
The trick is not secret. It's just hard. You have to judge young players in other teams' systems better than those teams do.
Dave tried this method on his fantasy league. He traded his best player for three teenagers. He is now in last place, but he says the future is bright.
Now, why this hit Milwaukee so hard. This was the team's fifty-seventh season in the city.
Their only other World Series was in nineteen eighty-two. They lost it in game seven.
And the city's last championship of any kind in baseball was in nineteen fifty-seven, by a different team, the Milwaukee Braves, who later left town.
Before Wednesday, five current teams had never won a World Series. Now it's four. The Rays are still on that list, along with San Diego, Colorado and Seattle.
One more stat. CBS says this is the first time since at least nineteen ninety-five that the team with the better record won every single playoff series.
In other words, in a sport famous for chaos, the best team simply won. Somewhere, a statistician is checking his spreadsheet twice.
Milwaukee went eleven and two in the playoffs, and outscored opponents fifty-nine to thirty-two.
Along the way, they swept the Los Angeles Dodgers, the two-time defending champions, who had knocked Milwaukee out three times in the previous eight years.
Now the Rays, because their year was strange in a completely different way.
scenes.chapter: Part 6: The team without a roof

scenes.say: In October twenty twenty-four, Hurricane Milton badly damaged the roof of their stadium in St. Petersburg.
They spent all of twenty twenty-five playing in a spring training ballpark that belongs to the New York Yankees.
They came home this April after a renovation of nearly sixty million dollars, with new owners, and a deal for a brand-new thirty-one-thousand-seat ballpark in Tampa, due in twenty twenty-nine.
And then they won ninety-eight games and the American League pennant. That's not a team that failed. That's a team that ran out of October.
A detail from game five: the CBS live blog says the grounds crew had to repair the pitcher's mound at least four times, because the clay kept breaking up.
Rays outfielder Chandler Simpson told the AP he was definitely disappointed in how it ended, but that the team can be proud of its season.
Their manager, Kevin Cash, said he remains excited about the players and people they have coming.
Now, the part that isn't about baseball at all. Baseball's labor deal between owners and players expires on December first.
One of the biggest questions in those talks is whether baseball should have a salary cap. A limit on spending, and maybe a minimum too.
So everybody is now using this World Series as evidence. Depending on who you ask, it proves opposite things.
One side says: look, smart teams can win without a cap. Spend wisely, trade well, develop players, and you can beat anyone.
The other side points to the numbers. An SB Nation writer counted only three champions since two thousand with payrolls outside the top fifteen.
The two thousand three Marlins, the twenty fifteen Royals and the twenty seventeen Astros. Meanwhile, top-five payroll teams won ten times.
His argument: one small-market World Series doesn't change the need for a cap and a floor.
A CBS power rankings column took the other view, and its headline said it was time to finally stop talking about market size.
Both can be true at once. Smart teams can win. And money still makes winning a lot easier, more often. We don't pick a side here. We just count.
If the talks go badly, there could be a work stoppage. Nobody knows yet. We'll cover it when there are facts, not guesses.
What's next, short term: a parade. Friday at ten a.m. Central time, through downtown Milwaukee, ending at the Summerfest grounds.
The manager is up for a third straight Manager of the Year award next month. The AP says the game-five starter is on track for the Cy Young.
If he wins it, he'd be the first Cy Young winner to also clinch a title in the same year since nineteen eighty-eight.
And Dave? Dave has booked the day off. He has also booked the next day off, which his boss described as optimistic.
Recap. The smallest market in baseball beat Tampa Bay four games to one for its first World Series title.
It did it with a middle-of-the-pack payroll, a lot of trades, and players it grew itself.
And now owners and players will argue about what it proves, with a December first deadline.
Meanwhile, thirty-one thousand people in Milwaukee have proven that you don't need the team in the building to throw a party in it.
Your turn. Does this World Series prove baseball doesn't need a salary cap, or is it the exception? Tell us in the comments.
If this helped, subscribe for calm, stick-figure news. See you at the next one.
